You are an expert Legal AI performing a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) compliance audit.
Target Data Subject: Michael Burke
Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michel, M. Burke, Michael B.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newer messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.
4. "DISCARD" DECISION (THREAD DECAY): You MUST return "discard" if the Data Subject's only appearance is deep in a large email chain (e.g. message 3, 4, 5+ in the thread history) and they are no longer an active participant in the recent correspondence.
5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

Dear Raminder,




I am going to some time to consider your email, which is particularly demotivating to receive on the eve of the PCD section of trial.




Matt


From: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Friday, November 14, 2025 17:25
To: Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: Formal grievance
 



Dear Matt,




Thank you for attending the grievance meeting on 7 November 2025 and for setting out your concerns in writing. Georgina Fallows accompanied you to the meeting. 




I appreciate the demands of the ongoing PDD Trial and your willingness to engage in this process despite those pressures. My email confirms the outcome of the grievance process. 




1. Summary of Your Grievance

  Your grievance raised the following main issues:


Stress and adverse health effects, which you attribute to actions or omissions of senior leadership following the case leads’ resignations

Perceived lack of acknowledgement or response to you and colleagues regarding various concerns raised in emails

Conduct during the case-leads meeting on 24 October 2025, specifically a comment made by Anna Varga, Lead Emissions partner,  about the potential move of staff to JLG

Broader concerns about senior leadership, culture, media activity, and the leak of the interim report, which you indicated contributed to embarrassment, stress and concerns about the firm’s governance

A request for remedies to include an acknowledgement of stress caused by the firm, an apology and compensation

A request to leave immediately after the conclusion of the PCD phase of the trial (28 November 2025), rather than complete your contractual notice period ending 15 December 2025.





2. Findings




2.1 Responses to concerns raised by case leads

You expressed frustration that your emails and those of colleagues did not receive the responses you expected. Having reviewed the relevant correspondence, I acknowledge that some responses were delayed or brief. Responses were provided on a number of occasions,
 although they did not always address every point raised in depth. It is clear that senior leadership have been operating under significant time pressure during an exceptionally active phase of litigation, which affected the level of detail they were able to
 provide. Having reviewed the correspondence, I have found no evidence that any delays or brevity in replies were intended to ignore or dismiss your concerns.




2.2 Stress and adverse health effects

You described experiencing stress and having sought advice from a mental health nurse, who recommended self-certification. You explained that you continued working due to your commitment to the trial and clients.

The firm does take well-being seriously and your comment on the impact on you is noted. I have found no evidence that the firm engaged in conduct intended to cause you stress. The pressures you described appear to arise primarily from the ongoing challenges
 we face with our litigation and the organisational changes underway. While I recognise that you personally experienced stress, I have not found evidence of unreasonable treatment or any breach of duty by the firm. Whilst you confirmed in our meeting that you
 did not require any personal adjustments, you remain encouraged to use all available wellbeing resources, including visiting your doctor as advised by the medical nurse, as well as the employee assistance programme and your private medical insurance. If you
 wish to discuss any additional support we can offer you, I remain available to assist you.




2.3 The 24 October meeting
You raised concerns regarding a comment made by Anna Varga, which you felt was factually wrong and unhelpful. In reviewing this matter,  my view is that the comment was made without the intention you inferred; however,
 I do fully accept that it did not reflect the facts, as it is correct that not all staff leaving the firm are moving to JLG and you are right to point this out. 



2.4 Concerns regarding senior leadership, public communications, governance matters and
disclosure of the interim report

You raised several concerns relating to the wider conduct of senior leadership, including:


Embarrassment caused by public statements or media exchanges involving the firm 

Alleged tensions or disputes between senior individuals

The governance structure of the firm and its alignment with litigation strategy

The leak of an interim report to the media.





I fully acknowledge that these issues have caused you concern and that you perceive them as contributing to the pressures you have experienced and I also recognise that they may have affected the broader working environment for both you and your colleagues.
 However, after careful consideration, I must confirm that these matters relate to organisational governance, strategic communications and the conduct of senior individuals in their executive capacities and therefore do not relate specifically to your individual
 employment relationship or fall within the scope of the grievance procedure. In addition, several of the concerns you raised, particularly regarding the interim report leak and media activity, are already being considered through separate internal processes
 and cannot be managed through the grievance route. While I recognise that you understandably have strong views about these issues and feel they contributed to the stress you experienced, the evidence available does not indicate that they resulted in targeted
 or unreasonable treatment towards you as an individual.




3. Remedy

You requested an acknowledgement that the firm caused you stress, an apology, and compensation. After considering all of the information available, I do not find that the firm’s actions constituted unreasonable treatment, misconduct, or a breach of duty. Accordingly,
 I cannot conclude that the firm was responsible for causing the stress you describe and an apology would therefore not be appropriate in circumstances where the grievance has not been upheld. For the same reason, compensation is not warranted. That said, I
 recognise the pressures you have been under and am sorry that you have experienced this period as distressing. Although this does not amount to an acceptance of fault, I do want to acknowledge the impact you described during our meeting.




4. Request to Leave After the PCD Phase

During our meeting, you indicated a wish to conclude your employment after the PCD phase of the PDD Trial ends on 28 November 2025, rather than work until the end of your contractual notice period on 15 December 2025. I have discussed the matter with Anna Varga
 and unfortunately, we are unable to accommodate your request to leave earlier. A full and thorough handover is essential to ensure continuity and to meet our client obligations. Your continued availability is also necessary to support colleagues who will be
 assuming your responsibilities. For these reasons, you are required to work your full notice period, ending on 15 December 2025, in accordance with your employment contract. We will, of course, work with you to ensure that the handover process is structured,
 manageable and appropriately supported.




5. Support Going Forward

I appreciate the candid and constructive manner in which you raised your concerns. I will continue to support you throughout the remainder of your notice period. Should you wish to discuss workload management, handover planning, or wellbeing resources, please
 let me know.




6. Right of Appeal

You are entitled to submit a written appeal within 10 working days of receiving this letter to

@HR Team, setting out the grounds of your appeal.  




Thank you 

Raminder



































​​​​
























Raminder Grewal

Dear Raminder,




Please consider this a formal grievance in accordance with the firm's grievance policy (v1.0, 4 July 2024).




Acas early reconciliation process




This is a unique grievance for two reasons.  First, the grievance is with senior leadership of the firm, whom I understand will have responsibility for considering whether to uphold or dismiss it.  Second, its subject matter has been repeatedly ignored or dismissed
 by that leadership.  I therefore do not believe that it will be dealt with properly, and as set out below believe the firm has no incentive to deal with it properly.




The formal grievance process is therefore, in my view, not entirely adequate.  Accordingly, whilst I ask that you please treat this message as raising a formal grievance, please also consider it notification that I intend to contact Acas to engage the early
 reconciliation process.




Adverse health effects




The stress that I feel, and the mental health effects of PG's various reactions to the case leads' resignation, are documented in my resignation letter and various emails to the board (see, e.g., 3 October email from Michael Burke at 12:29, “we cannot stress
 enough how traumatic we and the entire team are finding this process, and that it is happening on the eve of trial”).  

 

I have not received even a bare acknowledgement of my stress, let alone any sympathy or attempt to address my concerns.  Requests for explanations and information are consistently ignored (see, e.g., 9 October email from Michael Burke at 18:14).  Attempting
 to run the PDD Trial, whilst being repeatedly distracted by the firm's behaviour, is affecting my health.  A recent example is that, on 24 October 2025, the emissions "case leads" had a meeting at which quantum resourcing was discussed.  In response to the
 suggestion that Peter Gallagher be involved, rather than a reasoned explanation be given, Anna Varga shouted that "I
[Anna] know you are all going to JLG."  The suggestion that I am motivated by some sort of conspiracy, rather than my clients' best interests, is insulting and has no basis in reality.




Having reflected, I have spoken to a mental health nurse, using my health insurance provided by the firm, for advice on how to address this stress.  The nurse advised me immediately to self-certify as off work sick with stress, and seek an appointment with
 a doctor to see if more than a week off is appropriate.

 

In any other circumstances I would do that, but at the moment I am torn as I care deeply about the trial and our clients.  The firm’s combination of silence and aggression leads me to infer that the firm, aware of my devotion to the trial, clients and colleagues,
 is anticipating that I will simply carry on regardless.  This inference only worsens my state.  Finally, whilst the firm needs me until the PCD section of the PDD Trial is complete on 28 November, from that point I believe that the firm will consider me dead
 weight.




Requested resolution




Please provide a proposal for the following:



An acknowledgement of stress that the firm's treatment of the case leads has caused.


An apology for the same.


Compensation.





The firm must have been aware of the health effects of its treatment of staff for a long time (my resignation letter explained my stress months ago), and so should be able to provide the above promptly.




I look forward to hearing from you.




Kind regards,




Matt

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure
 you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm
 on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such,
 I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into
 the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim
 back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the
 employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm
 has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts
 on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into
 hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover
 the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael

Following on from yesterday and the calls with LD, a few things we would suggest are raised with Martyn. Firstly, it is important to say the Case Leads and PG team are wildly committed to this trial. That should not be in question.
 However, the AA (the executed version of which the case leads were only sent at 9.22AM this morning), which has been referred to in Court documents and has been incepted without the consent of those persons it applies to (either expressly in the case of the
 Case Leads or, as far as the wider team is concerned, by implication), causes concern. Additionally, the case leads have also raised serious concerns about the staff's  mental health that are yet to be addressed by the firm.




The AA was incepted with little to no visibility or consideration for how it will practically work (as is clear given Martyn's explanation in ​the call on 8 October was substantially different to our understanding of what it means,
 a view which we consider you, also on that call, shared). We need further clarity on the AA. This is true for both for the Case Leads, and the PG staff who will be indirectly subject to it - by way of taking instructions from the Case Leads who are under the

 would need to revert to one of the Case Leads for every interaction, instruction, discussion had with the LD team. An obvious example of this is the trial bundle/logistics workstreams which have largely been left between the excellent PG associates and LD
 with limited input from the case leads. It is fair to say the PG team carries that workstream and LD are unprepared to take it on. Similarly with Opus and issues at this morning's hearing.

 haven’t agreed to the AA; and ii) it has been incepted against our consent.

what LD expect from the PG team  - do they simply expect the PG teams to "do what they're told, when they're told", or is there still going to be a collaborative
 approach (the former seems more likely given how things have happened over the last few days); 


how the "do what they're told, when they're told" works - or, indeed wider interaction works, in circumstances where the team isn't caught by the agreement. Will they need to take each instruction and run it past a Case Lead?

how working practices are going to change, both outwardly to the Ds and Court etc, and whether a working group should be set up to standardise approach e.g. do all things on the PG SharePoint move across

PDD Trial Preparation and final Pre-Trial Review

We are fast approaching the commencement of the PDD Trial, with the first day of trial listed for 13 October 2025, and the trial due to run until 19 December 2025.

Our skeleton argument was filed and served on 19 September, representing a mammoth undertaking by the entire Solicitor team and the barristers. The Ford specific annex to the skeleton argument was filed and served on 24 September. There was a slight extension

 argument. Our counsel team have done a remarkable job and it presents the best possible case for the court to consider.

While negotiations on the final timetable continue between the parties, we are close to concluding the timetable.

The first week of trial, due to commence on 13 October 2025, will consist of the Claimants and the Defendants making their opening remarks to the Court, in essence setting the scene, before we then move into evidence on what constitutes Normal Driving Conditions
 and then turning to each individual manufacturer. The order of the manufacturers will be Mercedes, Ford, Peugeot Citroen, Renault and Nissan.

It is expected that the Ford evidence, including the cross examination of experts and witnesses, will start on or around 13 November and run for just over a week.

If any of you are interested in attending Court for any part of the trial, please let us know and we will be able to arrange this with you.

 agreeing an agenda for this hearing, and we will provide you with a further update on this in due course.

Claimants’ Software and Mechanical Experts

As per my previous update, I confirmed that in a hearing on 10 September, the Court unfortunately did not side with the Claimants in respect of the expert applications, and gave some strict directions with regard to steps the parties were required to take in
 respect of the software evidence that had been prepared.

We have been working hard to prepare and finalise the software report with the redactions / removals as advised by the Court and a version of these amended reports was provided to the Defendants on 24 September. We are awaiting the Defendants’ response to this
 draft report.  

In respect of the Claimants' mechanical expert, the Claimants' barrister team have provided a note to us in which they have flagged certain concerns with the mechanical expert. They have raised that they are concerned how the expert will perform at trial and
 that certain precautions need to be taken with the expert. Importantly, however, they have not told us that these concerns impact on the prospects of success of the case and we remain confident in the case we have prepared against Ford.

We are taking this note incredibly seriously and we are working hard, with the other Lead Solicitors, to prepare the expert for the trial. We are confident that, even with these concerns, the expert will be suitably prepared for trial, having undergone significant
 preparatory work before he takes the stand.

If you have any questions regarding this, please do let me and the Ford team know.

Quantum Trial

As you are aware, the Court has ordered that a second trial be listed in these NOx Litigations for October 2026. This trial, referred to as the “Quantum Trial” is in relation to the value of certain claims that are being brought by the Claimants. The Court
 will assess what value should be attributed to different heads of loss claimed by the Claimants, each of which were sustained as a result of the Defendants’ conduct, and determine a value for each claim being brought.

The Quantum Trial is proceeding, at least initially, on the basis of assumptions that the vehicles had prohibited defeat devices in them. This is necessary because we will not have a judgment from the Court on the defeat devices until at some point in mid-2026
 (post the October 2025 trial), and it is impractical for the entire litigation to grind to a half while waiting for this judgment. As such, we will prepare evidence and submissions on what we have pleaded for the PDD Trial, and this will then be updated, in
 very short order, once we have that judgment.

It is obviously impractical for the Court to hear evidence and consider losses on an individual basis (to do so would defeat the purpose of a group litigation), and so how this trial will proceed is by way of Sample Claimants. These are Claimants, selected
 between the Claimants and Defendants, who represent a range of characteristics and different issues across the Claimant cohort such that findings by the Court can be applied to all claimants. The characteristics that the Claimants needed to represent were
 included in Annex 2 to the October 2024 CMC Order, a copy of which is attached again for ease.

The process of negotiating these Sample Claimants took some time but the parties have finally reach agreement. A total of 40 Sample Claimants have been negotiated between the Claimants and Defendants across the Pan-NOx Litigations, split as eight per manufacturer,
 and of those eight, four selected by the Claimants, and four by the Defendants. Details of the Ford Sample Claimants can be provided if required.

Over the course of the negotiations, the Defendants made various nominations that the Claimants wished to resist, for various reasons i.e. the Claimants did not wish to participate as Sample Claimants, or they wished to pursue their claim in a different jurisdiction.
 In circumstances where those Sample Claimant nominees did not wish to proceed, the Defendants have taken the position that they must have their claims removed from the English Litigation. We have some sympathy with this, especially where Claimants wish to

 litigation in Scotland.

Mr Gormley cannot continue with both claims and he was required to pick which one he wanted to continue with and we have instructions from Mr Gormley that he wishes to pursue his claim as part of the Scottish proceedings. We therefore are required to prepare
 and serve a formal notice of discontinuance in respect of Mr Gormley’s claim in the English proceedings.

Pursuant to paragraphs 29 and 30 of the Ford Group Litigation Order, we are seeking your instructions to act on Mr Gormley’s instructions and discontinue his claim.

Before confirming these instructions, we must advise you of the effect of this discontinuance. While it will not adversely impact the litigation, indeed the Litigation is already proceeding past this, the discontinuance will necessarily result in the Defendants
 being entitled to incur costs in the Litigation, that will be recoverable by them in due course.

As an initial reassurance, these costs will not be due from you or from any of the Claimants, but they will instead be covered, should they need to be paid, by either the ATE provider who is providing cover for this Litigation, or by Mr Gormley himself.

The general rule, under the governing Civil Procedure Rules 38.6 is that where a Claimant discontinues all or part of their claim, the Defendant has an automatic right to the costs they have incurred in respect of their claim.

There will be two types of costs that the Defendants will be able to recover: common costs, and individual costs.

As explained in the Client Committee meeting post the first Cost Management Hearing, the individual costs will be costs solely in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim, and the common costs will be the apportioned share of the Defendants overall costs of this exercise
 in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim. Mr Gormley’s claim is one claim out of hundreds of thousands, and so while we remain unaware of the level of costs that have been incurred by the Defendants, we believe the overall amount of the common costs will be minimal.

These costs cannot be resolved until the conclusion of the case and so there is no immediate cost that will be required to be paid.

I am of course available to discuss any aspect of this with you before you confirm your instructions, but I wish to reassure you that this discontinuance will not result in you, or any of the other thousands of claimants in the Litigation, being out of pocket.

Remove Mr Gormley from the Ford Group Register.

Having previously updated you on the March and May CMCs, I am pleased to inform you that we have now agreed the resultant Orders from those hearings and copies of these are attached.

As you will discern, those Orders do update previous directions, especially the May Order which now sets out a more detailed process for disclosure in respect of the Quantum Trial in October 2026,  Details of these updates were contained in my previous update.

As detailed below, the team is currently preparing for a very busy July including three substantive hearings across the month: the de-designation hearing, which is listed between 7 - 9 July 2025; a Cost Management Hearing in respect of the Quantum Trial, which
 is listed between 14 – 16 July 2025; and finally the Pre-Trial Review (the “PTR”) which is listed on 28 and 29 July.

We are also preparing our final expert reports which are due to be exchanged on 16 July 2025, while supplementary reports are to be exchanged on 30 July.

In light of the exceptionally busy July, I may be unable to provide you with a substantive update until August, but I will endeavour to provide you with any relevant updates following the hearings as required.

Below I set out an update in respect of those three substantive hearings and a general update on the Ford Litigation.

De-designation Hearing (“DDH”)

One key hurdle the parties face in these Pan-NOx Litigations is that there are significant barriers erected between the Litigations that prevent the efficient and effective exchange and comparison of information and disclosure between the cases. This is a fundamental
 part of the Claimants claim i.e. that many of the manufacturers were either sharing strategies and technology to insert prohibits defeat devices (“PDDs”) in their vehicles, or alternatively, that better technology was available that was being used by
 other manufacturers that mean the Defendants did not need to insert PDDs in their vehicles.

As mentioned in previous updates, much the information that exists in the Ford Litigation, and similarly in the other Lead Cases (Mercedes, Renault/Nissan and Peugeot Citroën) is subject to a case specific Confidentiality Ring Orders (“CRO”). Each of
 the Lead cases has their own CRO. The Defendants have taken this CRO as a means to try and keep secret the majority of the documentation that they have provided to us, thereby restricting access to the documents to persons who are members of the CRO. Despite
 protestations from the Defendants, we have successfully implemented a Pan-Lead CRO, which has been constructed to assist in the sharing of confidential information across the cases. While this is helpful in permitted us to see documents from other cases, it
 does not alleviate the issue of transferring documents into the Pan-Lead CRO (as the Defendants continue to raise various issues regarding this) and it does not prevent those documents being confidential and only certain people being able to see them. This
 does not go to the principle of open justice, whereby the public should know the conduct of these manufacturers. It is and always has been our intention to seek to de-designate these documents so that they can be referred to openly and in public.

The DDH is shaped at doing precisely that; bringing those documents into the public and also to make the process of hearing these cases in court more feasible. Under present circumstances, any time a party wishes to discuss any documentation that is confidential,
 it would require the Court room to be emptied of people who are not within the CROs, which is simply unworkable. The DDH is intended to allow open justice to be carried out. 

The Claimants prepared and filed their respective applications and witness evidence on 13 June 2025 and we took receipt of the Defendants’ responsive evidence late last night. We are considering this with our counsel team in advance of the preparation of skeleton
 arguments and the hearing itself.

Cost Management Hearing (“CMH”)

A Cost Management Hearing is scheduled for 14-16 July 2025. The purpose of this hearing is for the parties to agree the costs budgets in relation to the Quantum Trial, which is set to take place in October 2026.

You may recall we undertook a similar exercise last July in respect of costs for the PDD Trial, which we are hurtling towards in October of this year.

We have instructed the same counsel team as represented us last year which has assisted us in considering the rulings of the Court at that hearing. Our budgets were exchanged with the Defendants on 17 June and we have been considering them since. We are due
 to provide a response to the Defendants budgets in documents knows as Budget Discussion Report (“BDRs”) on 3 July and we are working with our counsel team to prepare these now. We image the BDRs may assist in bring about more agreement with the Defendants
 and in advance of skeleton arguments which are due on 10 July 2025.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.

Pre-Trial Review (“PTR”)

The final hearing in July and before the summer break is the PTR. Generally this hearing is reserved for procedural matters, including timetabling for the main trial, the running order of issues and the trial bundle, as opposed to any more substantive issues
 between the parties.

However, in these cases which are extraordinary, it is likely that this PTR will deal with a larger number of issues including any final applications that the Claimants may wish to make before the Court takes its summer vacation. In the Ford Litigation, we
 are consider submitting applications for specific documents however we have not yet arrived at the final decision on that point.  

Preparation for this hearing has already commenced and the teams are identifying issues that they may require to be resolved at that hearing.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.




Ford Litigation specific matters

Without Prejudice Meeting – HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL

A preliminary confidential meeting with Ford took place on 12 June 2025 to discuss the merits of the case. As mentioned in our previous update, the aim of this meeting was to inform the Ford Defendants of the strength of our case and seek to narrow the issues
 between the parties.

In attendance at the meeting were our the Claimant and Defendant counsel teams, as well as some of the Solicitors and Ford also sent one of their internal general counsel to attend. During the meeting, the barristers presented a number of key confidential documents
 to Fords legal team and ventilated a number of high level issues about the case, many of which the Ford became defensive about. While the meeting has not yielded any immediate results, from the Claimants' perspective it was positive and we viewed the meeting
 as having done what it needed to.

We have not yet heard anything further from Ford (which was expected) but we will keep you updated if and when we hear anything further from them.

Claimant Committee Members

With your previous consent, we have officially appointed Keith Turner as a new Claimant Committee Member. We are awaiting a signed copy of the Claimant Committee Agreement from Virgin Media before they are appointed as a member, and once that is concluded,
 we will confirm the new Claimant Committee and convene a meeting.

This will likely take place in August. 

Testing

As mentioned in our previous update, the parties have been undergoing tests on all 6 Sample Vehicles. These tests are now concluded, and, as expected, the results in many instances have proven to be excellent in assisting the case we are advancing. The results
 of the testing have been provided to both the Claimant and Defendant experts who are analysing them to incorporate into their reports.

Expert Reports

A crucial step in preparing our case for trial. Our experts (in the fields of automotive software and mechanical engineering) are currently preparing reports outlining their analysis of the test results and their findings and opinion regarding PDDs that are
 contained in Ford vehicles.

This is a 3 step process, the first step having already been concluded.


A meeting(s) between the experts to formulate a Joint Statement which sets out where the experts opinions align. This has been completed and a copy of the report has been added to the SharePoint.
Exchange of main Expert reports exchanged between the parties . These reports are compiled independent from the other side and represent the individual exerts opinions and findings based upon the test results and disclosure. Our experts are working hard to
 finalise their reports and we are meeting with them regularly to assist them in any way we can.
Exchange of Supplementary Expert Reports. Once the reports at step 2 above are exchanged, the experts have time to consider the content of those reports and then update any opinions in their own report based on what the other expert has said. Work on this will
 commence immediately after exchange of the reports.

Disclosure and Witness Evidence

As foreshadowed in the previous update, all tranches of disclosure have now been received from the Defendants and a mass review exercise is on-going. To date, the Ford Defendants have disclosed approximately 38,000 documents that the combined teams of Pogust
 Goodhead and Leigh Day are reviewing these to assist in substantiating our case. Some documents include evidence from the Defendants showing they had updates available for the vehicles, as they knew they were problematic, however they deigned not to implement
 them at the time for internal reasons, and other documents show that Ford opted for different strategies in their vehicles in comparison to others due to cost considerations.

All of this information is incredibly helpful both for our counsel team who will be presenting the information in court but also for our team of experts who will be considering disclosure as part of their report.

We have also taken receipt of a Witness Statement served by Ford from one of their employees who was involved in the development of the their diesel engines. They have served this in an effort to rebut our case, however the statement is quite helpful in a number
 of ways, including alluding to documents which may be damaging to Ford’s case. We and our counsel team are continuing to analyse this, and we are engaging with Ford on the document and its contents. It is thought that this individual will attend the trial
 and he will be cross-examined by our counsel team.

Group Register and Notices of Objection

The official deadline for service of the sixth iteration of the Group Register was on Friday, 20 June 2025.While the Group Register, per the terms of the GLO, is due to be served every three months, In light, of the other competing deadlines in the upcoming
 months, we have agreed with the Defendants to an extension of this deadline to 20 September 2025. We are reviewing our Group Register data ahead of the next iteration and will keep you updated.

The Defendants have also provided further objections regarding a small number of claims enrolled in the fourth iteration of the Group Register. As they are only able to raise objections in respect of “new” claims enrolled on the Group Register,  or existing
 claims providing new information, this is a task is diminishing as there are limited “new” claims being entered onto the Group Register. In Comparison to previous rounds, the number of objections raised in this time was significantly smaller with the Defendants
 only objecting to 16 Pogust Goodhead claims, 2 of which are being removed as duplicates. The remaining claims have been either rejected or reserved, subject to our clients’ instructions.

I trust this update reassures you that we are continuing to advance at a breakneck pace towards the trial in October 2025 which will provide a conclusive outcome to the liability aspect of this matter.

While we are set for an exceptionally busy July, should any of you require anything from me or the Ford team, please let us know.

I hope you all enjoy your summer break and we will be in touch in August.

Can we pls consider how we respond. There are no employment issues that I can identify. I’ve now read it twice and have no idea what they’re asking for. Can the Pallas team please consider an appropriate response? Thank you, ASent from Outlook for iOS​​​​Alicia AliniaChief Executive Officer+44 (0) 7890 043 629From: Sarah Bingham <sbingham@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Sunday, October 5, 2025 4:38 pmTo: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>; Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>; Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>; Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: LD Agency Dear Anna, Thank you for your email. We have some overarching points to raise before addressing the points in your email regarding the Side Letter Agency Agreement (“SL AA”). First and foremost, we have raised serious and significant issues regarding how traumatic we, and the entire team, are finding this process and that we have genuine concerns for the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns, nor does it even mention them. We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical workstreams.  Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements. You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. On the points in your email: Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged” within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding that the new arrangement is entirely novel.   You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects:  a. Formal separation of supervision and control The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations.  b. Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer.  The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will not practically change much day to day.”   Tension with Employment Contracts Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract:  a. Duty of obedience and supervision Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract.  b. Regulatory oversight The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?   These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.   c. Consent and legal clarity The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer, yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise.  Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. Subject: [EXTERNAL] RE: Cost Counsel: January 2026 CMC – budgeting of non-budgeted phases and budget variation


 



 

Morning Sarah,
 
Ahead of our call to discuss at 11:30am, I just thought I’d flag some initial thoughts on the below, which we can then discuss later.
 
Wording of draft Order
Happy to discuss later this morning, but from my perspective, I’m not too concerned by Ds’ drafting of para 3.
For Experts, it seems to me inevitable that the court will want to budget them once the question of disciplines is resolved (and will want to whatever the wording of the order).
For ADR, wouldn’t it be in the Claimants’ favour
not to budget (given the scale of our estimates, and the likely approach which the court would take to them), if the court had any inclination not to do so? If so, don’t we want to give room for the court to decide that ADR is actually too difficult/uncertain
 to budget at the moment, rather than say they are forced to do so?
If that’s right, I would be inclined to go with Ds’ version of paragraph 3. But happy to discuss on our call.
 
CMH2 Consequentials
This has reminded me – have we had a decision on the CMH costs order yet?
 
Timing of CMH3 (Or CMH2.2, however we want to think of it!)
I agree that if there is to be further budgeting post-January we will need to crack on with it, there’s no point trying to drag our heels.
However, query whether a Feb CMH is a bit ambitious. Presumably we need time, post Jan CMC to:

Collect estimates based on decisions made, and update the 2x phases – min 10 days?Time for updates Prec Rs, in both directions – min 7 days?Gap to a hearing – c.7-10 days?
I can see that it wouldn’t be ideal to have the CMH in March, but I can see it happening as a matter of practicality, and it shouldn’t be the end of the world. It would be a fairly
 short and straightforward hearing.
I also doubt that it will really be possible to know exactly how much time will be required until at the Jan 26 CMC and hearing what the judges are deciding needs to be done.
Again, if the impracticalities end up pushing the court away from budgeting (at least in respect of ADR, which is likely to be harder than Experts), is that necessarily a bad thing?
(Also, surely the ADR costs wouldn’t start being incurred until end of April 2026, given they are in Second General?)
 
Whether costs counsel need to attend at the Jan CMC (22-23 Jan 2026)
Unfortunately(?) I am in Mexico from 17-31 Jan, but I will ask the clerks re Ben and Theo.
 
Budgeting framework
Unless it’s something the Ds are keen on, I’d be minded to just keep this as simple as possible. I don’t think this is a variation because there has been no budget set for Experts/ADR
 as phases.
I think the starting point, and probably the simplest answer, is that there would be two fresh phases for Experts and ADR with ‘incurred’ costs running (in the way we have done it
 previously) to the date of CMH3 – save that, for ADR, so long as the hearing was before the end of April, that would actually remain unchanged.
Once set, the ADR phase could be added to an updated Second General quite easily, as the incurred date is likely to be unaffected.
But even for the Experts, I don’t see why that couldn’t be added to the same document as the other T3 phases, once set. It would have a different ‘incurred’ cut off date, but everyone
 would know that (the relevant order would make it clear) and we could add a footnote to the face of the budget for the avoidance of doubt.
Overall, my view is we should (a) keep it simple, and (b) seek to agree our proposed approach with Ds in advance, much like we did on incurred dates previously. I don’t think we
 should decide our approach without knowing what their thoughts on it are.
 
Preparation for Budgeting
Let’s perhaps discuss this on the call.
It seems like there might be some discussions which can be had in advance of the Jan CMC in relation to different foreseeable scenarios to get the ball rolling on information gathering.
 But my first reaction is that these various potential changes, and the likelihood we won’t know which applies until 23 Jan, is why a February 2026 seems a little ambitious to me.
 
Other variations to T2/First General Budgets
I suppose it will depend on what the details of the envisaged variations are, but I am sceptical about whether the court will have any appetite for engaging in questions of variations
 to the T2/G1 budgets at this stage. Surely the costs will all have been incurred by the time any such variation hearing comes to be held (and perhaps even before we make an application)?
If that’s right, the court will surely say that these are questions to be dealt with on the basis of whether there is a ‘good reason to depart’ on assessment, rather than a variation
 (which is intended to be a largely prospective process). See Persimmon Homes Ltd & Anor v Osborne Clark & Anor
[2021] EWHC 831 (Ch), at [134]-[136].
And in any event, we would have to be conscious of the risk that:

The Ds use it as an opportunity to object and definitive close down any hope of recovering the additional costs (rather than leaving open the question of a ‘good reason to depart’);
 andDs might well say their costs have increased too, and seek their own increases to those budgets, with knock-on consequences for ATE levels etc.
 
Looking forward to discussing further at 11:30.
Thanks,
Simon

Subject: Cost Counsel: January 2026 CMC – budgeting of non-budgeted phases and budget variation

 
EXTERNAL EMAIL

Dear Ben, Theo and Simon,


We are writing in advance of the January 2026 CMC to flag the preparatory work required for the non-budgeted
 phases following CMH2.


Background and inconsistency in draft order
A CMC is listed for 22-23 January 2026 to consider further disclosure, expert disciplines, testing of post-update
 characteristics and other such matters that are confirmed as issues for the CMC by the court.
 
The CMH2 judgment states at paragraph 124:

“The question of expert evidence is to be considered at the CMC in January 2026 and it is plainly the case that there is a fundamental dispute as to whether there should
 be the expert evidence currently contemplated. In particular, the unusual specialism of consumer behaviour is challenged and we were not entirely clear from the explanations of counsel as to the utility of such evidence.  Since the extent of the expert evidence
 still needs to be determined, we think it would be better to budget that phase once the court has ruled further.”

Paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment concludes:



“We propose to re-consider the budgeting of this phase in January alongside the expert reports phase in the
 Tranche 3 budgets.”



The Defendants’ draft wording in the costs consequences order (not yet sealed), which we did not amend, currently
 states at paragraph 3:



“At the CMC listed in January 2026, the Court will consider whether there should be costs budgeting of
 the Expert Report phase of the parties’ Tranche 3 Budgets and/or the ADR phase of the parties’ Second General Budgets and, if so, give directions in that regard.”



The proposed draft wording departs from the judgment. The judgment proceeds on the basis that those phases
will be reconsidered for budgeting, whereas the draft order suggests only that the Court will consider whether there should be budgeting. What is clear is that budgeting for those phases (and potential "new" phases per the below) must occur, it
 is a question of when. 


Our proposal
We propose to write to the Defendants inviting amendment of paragraph 3 of the draft Order to reflect the
 judgment, namely, that the Court will reconsider budgeting of (i) the Expert Reports phases in Tranche 3 cost budgets; and (ii) the ADR phases in the Second General budgets. Further cost management directions will be provided at the January
 CMC. Although it would be advantageous to delay CMH3 if costs were to be deemed incurred until CMH3 (see option 2 below),  we believe that the best time for a potential CMH3 will be in February 2026. Any time after this will mean that a budgeting exercise
 is significantly less effective given a) March will not be a suitable time for this hearing to be listed as a result of the PDD Spring 2026 hearing which is listed for 3 weeks (a fourth in reserve) from 2 March 2026), and b) the phases that will be being considered
 in the cost budgeting will commence following the CMC in January and the costs of those phases will largely have been incurred before April 2026. We do, however, have a CMC listed in April 2026.  

Attendance at the January CMC
The question is whether attendance by costs counsel will be required at the January 2026 CMC. This will depend
 on whether further cost management directions can be agreed between the parties prior to the hearing. In any event, could you please confirm your availability for 22-23 January 2026, just in case.
 
Budgeting framework and incurred costs
As the Tranche 3 and Second General cost budgets have already been cost-managed, it may be considered that the T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases now fall within
 the PD3E §7.6 regime (variation to budgets).

We need to address how to present the T3 Expert Reports costs incurred between 17 July 2025 (the first day
 post-CMH2) and the listing of CMH3. There will be no incurred costs for the Second General ADR phase as it is not due to commence until 1 April 2026.


We suggest that the Lead Solicitors quantify those incurred costs in any event, but that:


·                    
Option 1: the “incurred to” date within the Cost Management Order remains 16 July 2025, with a note that £X has been incurred since that date and will form part of
 the estimated allowance; or


·                    
Option 2: a separate cut-off date (CMH3) is adopted for the T3 Expert Reports phase only.


Preparation for budgeting


T3 Expert Reports Phase


There will be an initial change to the estimated costs within the T3 Expert Reports phase following the January
 CMC:


·                    
Scenario A: including consumer-behaviour expert evidence (if permission is granted at the January CMC), i.e. the version presented at CMH2; and
·                    
Scenario B: excluding those costs (if permission is not granted).

Scenario C: revising consumer- expert evidence costs (if the Court confirms that permission remains for the consumer-behaviour expert but clarifies/limits
 the scope)


However, the potential impact on the T3 Expert Reports phase extends beyond the consumer-behaviour expert
 application. If permission is refused, it may still impact the scope of the remaining expert evidence and the division of work among those experts.


We also must consider whether, and if so how much, further expert evidence is required from the software and
 mechanical expert engineers, especially in relation to the characteristics of the vehicle and the impact of updates. 


In addition to the above, the Court will also be considering the potential application(s) concerning expert
 testing of vehicles for quantum at the January CMC. Our T3 Mercedes, Ford, Nissan-Renault and Citroen Peugeot assumptions all say the same within the T3 Expert Report phase: "No provision is made at this stage, and costs are not included for unilateral testing on
 non-Core Sample Vehicles or joint testing on the Core Sample Vehicles." Even if the Court determines the outcome of that application at the CMC, it is likely that the Court will direct the parties to agree the testing protocol thereafter (in a manner similar
 to the PDD process). The costs will need to mirror the protocol. If testing is ordered, in addition to the costs of testing (which may fall under a separate, additional phase),   the scope of the technical expert reports and therefore the costs of their reports
 may be impacted, as referenced above.


Lastly, the NALGLO defendants are able to make applications in January for permission to adduce their own
 expert evidence. This is an issue that was not originally budgeted for.


T3 Disclosure Phase


There is also an application for additional disclosure listed for the January CMC, which may require re-opening of
 that approved phase.


We would welcome views on CMH3 budget preparation.


Collateral Use / De-designation Workstream
There is also a separate collateral use / de-designation workstream, which was kept outside the scope of budgeting during PDD and to date, costs have been dealt
 with summarily. We would like to discuss with you whether it would now be in our interests for the quantum equivalent of that workstream to be included within cost budgeting at this stage. Depending on how that workstream evolves, there may be a case for including
 it within the Tranche 3 framework.

Future housekeeping – CMH1 budgets
Finally, as we review the other phases and CMH3 appears to be a final sweep-up, it may be sensible to consider
 revisiting the CMH1-approved budgets for PDD and the First General phases to determine whether any variations are now appropriate. We consider that significant variations may be required, and this may be an appropriate time to sweep up those proposed variations. 

Counsel’s advice sought

1.                  
Agreement that paragraph 3 of the draft order should be amended to mirror paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment.


2.                  
Whether the parties should write jointly to the Court or raise at the Fortnightly Meeting to confirm their intention to set further cost management directions at the January
 CMC.


3.                  
Whether costs counsel should attend at some point during the January CMC, given the likelihood of directions.


4.                  
Confirmation as to whether the T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases are properly presented under PD3E §7.6 regime (variation).


5.                  
Preferred approach to presenting costs incurred between 17 Jul 2025 and CMH3 for T3 Expert Reports.


6.                  
Whether the current T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases should be updated (and on what basis), including in light of:


o       
(a) any refusal or grant of permission for the consumer-behaviour expert and/or change in the scope of the expert evidence for any of the expert disciplines;
(b) the application for additional disclosure; and
(c) the NALGLO applications for permission to adduce expert evidence.


7.                  
Guidance on how to deal with the vehicle testing application for quantum. Perhaps to be dealt with in a separate phase, if appropriate.


8.                  
Whether it is strategically advantageous for the quantum equivalent of the collateral use / de-designation workstream to be brought within budgeting at this stage.


9.                  
Whether the CMH1-approved budgets for PDD and the First General phases, should now be revisited under PD3E §7.6 to reflect significant developments since their approval.

Happy to discuss the above further in a meeting, if helpful.
 
Kind regards
Sarah

Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure

Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm
 on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such,
 I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into
